title: Pastry cream
subtitle: The base cream for choux buns, mille-feuille and Swiss cream, thickened with custard powder.
verified_note: Still being revised: the ratios and timings are going to be measured again.

result.note: Enough for 40 choux buns or one 24 cm mille-feuille base.

time.note: 20 min active (17 of them waiting for the milk to boil), then 45 min cooling in the fridge.

context: Pastry cream is milk thickened with custard powder. Because the starch is already in the powder, no egg yolks are needed and nothing can curdle: no tempering, far less risk of lumps. Two things make the difference. Stir the powder, the sugar and a splash of milk into a smooth paste first, otherwise the powder lumps in the hot milk. And let the cream boil briefly after it thickens: bind it too little and it is too thin to pipe, cook it too long and it turns rubbery.

melk.name: whole milk
melk.note: Whole milk gives the fullest flavour. Semi-skimmed or skimmed works too, and almond or soy milk if you want it plant-based.

roompoeder.name: custard powder
roompoeder.note: Sold as roompoeder or custard powder — the same product. The starch is already in it, so no eggs are needed and nothing can curdle. Check the label for a plant-based version: some brands contain milk powder.

suiker.name: sugar
suiker.note: Stirred into the custard powder with a splash of milk, not into the rest of the milk.

vanille.name: vanilla pod
vanille.note: Seeds and pod both go in. The pod stays in the cream until the end: it still has flavour to give.

stap-1.title: Custard powder, sugar and milk into a smooth paste
stap-1.text: Weigh out 50 g custard powder and 50 g sugar. Whisk in a small amount of milk until you have a smooth, lump-free paste.
stap-1.why: Powder that goes straight into hot milk lumps. A smooth paste beforehand is the whole secret behind a lump-free cream.
tips: Use a splash of the 500 g of milk for the paste; the rest goes into the pan.

stap-2.title: Warm the milk with the vanilla
stap-2.text: Pour the rest of the milk into the pan. Split the vanilla pod lengthways, scrape out the seeds and add seeds and pod to the milk.
stap-2.why: The flavour sits in the seeds and in the fatty parts around the pod; they need heat and time.
tips: Splitting the pod gets easier the more often you do it.
Leave the pod in; it can stay in the milk and in the cream until the end.

stap-3.title: Bring it to the boil
stap-3.text: Put the pan on medium heat and warm the milk to the boil, stirring with a spatula so the vanilla spreads through. Count on fifteen to twenty minutes.
stap-3.why: Keeping it moving stops a skin forming and spreads the vanilla evenly. This is the long step; the video does not cut it, so you can see how long it really takes.
tips: More heat is faster, but the milk will catch on the base — keep stirring and work quicker.
Any vanilla lumps you see will whisk out once the paste goes in.
In a hurry? Use the chapters to skip to the next step.

stap-4.title: The paste goes in, off the heat
stap-4.text: Take the pan off the heat as soon as the milk really boils. Pour the paste in while stirring — at least half of it, all of it is fine.
stap-4.why: Staying off the heat here is the difference between smooth and lumpy: the paste gets a moment to blend before the heat comes back.
tips: Stir while you pour, not afterwards.

stap-5.title: Back into the pan
stap-5.text: Stir everything back into the pan and return it to the heat, one setting lower than before.
stap-5.why: From here it goes fast: the starch thickens within a few minutes.
tips: Have a flat dish ready so you can pour it out straight away.

stap-6.title: Keep stirring until it is thick
stap-6.text: Keep stirring until the cream thickens and shows a few bubbles. Custard consistency is right.
stap-6.why: Stop stirring and you get lumps. Stop too early and the cream is too thin to pipe; cook it too long and it turns rubbery.
tips: Too thick? Stir a splash of extra milk through when you use it.
Too thin? Let it boil a little longer; thickening happens all at once.
Leave the vanilla pod in, now too.

stap-7.title: Pour out and cover
stap-7.text: Pour the cream straight into a flat dish — it cools faster. Put cling film directly onto the cream and chill for at least 45 minutes.
stap-7.why: Left in the pan it keeps cooking. And film on contact keeps air and moisture out, otherwise a skin forms that you can never stir smooth again.
tips: Do not stretch it over the rim of the dish: lay it on the cream itself.

0.q: Why custard powder and not eggs?
0.a: Custard powder already contains the starch. That means no yolks to temper and nothing that can curdle: fewer lumps and reliable thickening. Roompoeder is the same product under a different name.

1.q: Why will my cream not thicken?
1.a: Not long enough on the heat. It only thickens once it really boils: keep stirring until you see bubbles. Too thick, on the other hand, and a splash of milk at the end fixes it.

2.q: Why is there a skin on my cream?
2.a: No film, or film stretched over the rim instead of laid on the cream. Put the cling film directly on the surface.

3.a: Yes, with almond or soy milk. Do check the custard powder label: most are plant-based, some contain milk powder.

4.a: Three days in the fridge, covered on the surface. Do not freeze: the starch breaks down on thawing and the cream turns grainy.

0.oorzaak: the powder was not made into a paste first
0.fix: first make a smooth paste of the powder, the sugar and a splash of milk

1.fix: keep stirring until it really boils and shows bubbles

2.fix: stir a splash of extra milk through it when you use it

3.oorzaak: not covered on the cream itself
3.fix: cling film directly on the surface, not over the rim
